title: Central Forces and Central Field Mechanics
short_intro: A central force is a force whose line of action always passes through a fixed center point, and its magnitude depends solely on the distance from that center. Central forces are conservative in nature and possess spherical symmetry.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of central forces, proof of conservation of angular momentum under central forces, areal velocity constancy (Kepler's second law relation), and inverse-square law basics (gravitational and electrostatic forces).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Binet's differential equation of orbits, reduced mass transformation in two-body central force problems, effective potential energy curves, apsidal angles, and planetary motion stability.

prerequisites: Conservative force fields and potential energy
Conservation of linear and angular momentum

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Vector Representation
bullets: A force F(r) is termed a central force if it can be expressed mathematically as F(r) = f(r) r^, where r^ is the unit position vector and f(r) is a scalar function of the distance r from the center of force.
The line of action of the force vector always passes through the origin or the fixed center of attraction/repulsion.
Central forces are inherently spherically symmetric, meaning the force magnitude depends only on r = |r|, not on the angular coordinates (theta, phi).

concept_notes.heading: Conservation of Angular Momentum
bullets: Since the torque acting on a particle moving under a central force is zero (tau = r x F = r x f(r)r^ = 0), the angular momentum L of the particle remains strictly conserved.
Conservation of angular momentum dictates that the motion of the particle must be strictly confined to a fixed plane perpendicular to the constant vector L.
This planar restriction reduces the degrees of freedom from three (Cartesian coordinates x, y, z) to two (polar coordinates r, theta).

concept_notes.heading: Constancy of Areal Velocity
bullets: The areal velocity, defined as the rate at which the position vector sweeps out area (dA/dt), is directly proportional to the specific angular momentum L/m.
Areal velocity is given by dA/dt = L / (2m) = constant, which is a direct mathematical consequence of the conservation of angular momentum in a central field.
This principle forms the basis of Kepler's Second Law of planetary motion.

concept_notes.heading: Conservative Nature and Potential Energy
bullets: All central forces are conservative forces because the curl of F vanishes (nabla x F = 0).
A potential energy function V(r) can always be defined such that F(r) = - dV/dr r^.
The total mechanical energy E = T + V(r) remains constant throughout the motion of the particle in a central field.

derivations.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum and Planar Motion
derivations.conditions: Particle of mass m moving under any arbitrary central force F(r)r^
steps: Write the torque acting on the particle: tau = r x F = r x [f(r) r^].
Substitute r^ = r / r into the cross product: tau = r x [f(r) (r / r)] = [f(r) / r] (r x r).
Since the cross product of any vector with itself is zero (r x r = 0), the torque tau = 0.
By Newton's second law for rotation, tau = dL/dt = 0, which implies angular momentum L = r x p = constant.
derivations.result: L is a constant vector, proving that motion is confined to a fixed plane.

derivations.title: Binet's Equation for Orbit in Central Field
derivations.conditions: Particle under central force F(r), using transformation u = 1/r
steps: Express angular momentum in polar coordinates: L = m r^2 (d\theta/dt), giving d\theta/dt = L / (mr^2) = (L u^2)/m.
Substitute r = 1/u into radial equation of motion: m [d^2r/dt^2 - r (d\theta/dt)^2] = F(r).
Evaluate derivatives with respect to theta using chain rule: dr/dt = (dr/du)(du/d\theta)(d\theta/dt) = - (L/m) (du/d\theta).
Substitute derivatives back and simplify to obtain the differential equation for the orbit u(\theta).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effective Potential Energy vs Radial Distance (V_eff vs r)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve showing a potential well with a minimum point, having a steep centrifugal barrier term (1/r^2) dominating at small r and the attractive potential dominating at large r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The minimum of the effective potential curve corresponds to stable circular orbit radius. Horizontal lines representing total energy E indicate turning points (periapsis and apoapsis).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT to analyze stability of circular orbits and determine turning points of planetary motion.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kepler's Second Law Areal Sweep
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An elliptical orbit with the sun at one focus, showing two sectors swept out by the radius vector in equal time intervals with equal areas.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that equal areas are swept in equal times (dA/dt = constant), illustrating conservation of angular momentum.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested conceptually in TGT and PGT examinations regarding orbital speed variations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Planetary Orbit Geometry in Polar Coordinates
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An ellipse showing polar coordinates (r, theta) from the center of force (focus) to a point on the orbit, indicating perihelion r_min and aphelion r_max.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the inverse relationship between distance and orbital velocity due to angular momentum conservation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in numerical problem setup for calculating maximum and minimum velocities.

solved_numericals.question: A particle moves under the influence of a central force given by F(r) = - k / r^3. If the particle's mass is m and its angular momentum is L, find the differential equation of its orbit using substitution u = 1/r.
solution_steps: Recall Binet's formula: d^2u/d\theta^2 + u = - (m / (L^2 u^2)) * F(1/u).
Substitute F(1/u) = - k / (1/u)^3 = - k u^3 into the equation.
Simplify the right-hand side: - (m / (L^2 u^2)) * (- k u^3) = (m k u) / L^2.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass m moves in a circular orbit of radius r_0 under an attractive central force F(r) = - k / r^4. Find the condition for the stability of this circular orbit.
solution_steps: Write the effective potential for the force F(r) = - k / r^4. Since F(r) = - dV/dr, we have V(r) = - k / (3r^3).
For a circular orbit, the first derivative of V_eff with respect to r must vanish at r = r_0: dV_eff/dr|_{r=r_0} = \frac{k}{r_0^4} - \frac{L^2}{m r_0^3} = 0, which gives L^2 = \frac{mk}{r_0}.
For stability, the second derivative of V_eff must be greater than zero at r = r_0: d^2V_eff/dr^2|_{r=r_0} = -\frac{4k}{r_0^5} + \frac{3L^2}{m r_0^4} > 0.

Substitute L^2 = mk/r_0 into the second derivative condition: -\frac{4k}{r_0^5} + \frac{3(mk/r_0)}{m r_0^4} = -\frac{k}{r_0^5} > 0, which requires k < 0 (repulsive) or if attractive (k > 0), examine the exact inequality constraint: -4k + 3k < 0 => -k < 0, hence stable for specific power laws.
solved_numericals.answer: The circular orbit is stable if the effective potential curvature condition d^2V_{eff}/dr^2 > 0 is satisfied at r_0.

solved_numericals.question: If a particle describes a circular orbit of radius R under a central force F(r) = - \frac{k}{r^2}, find the total energy of the particle in terms of k and R.
solution_steps: For an inverse-square attractive force, potential energy is V(r) = - k / r.
From Newton's second law for circular motion: \frac{mv^2}{R} = \frac{k}{R^2}, which gives kinetic energy T = \frac{1}{2} mv^2 = \frac{k}{2R}.
Potential energy at r = R is V(R) = - \frac{k}{R}.

assumptions_and_limitations: The center of force is assumed to be stationary or located at the inertial frame origin (reduced mass is used if the center has finite mass).
Relativistic effects are ignored; classical mechanics formulations apply throughout.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All central forces are inverse-square forces.
common_misconceptions.correct: Inverse-square forces (like gravity and electrostatics) are only a specific subclass of central forces.
common_misconceptions.why: A central force can follow any functional dependence on distance, such as F(r) = -kr (Hooke's law) or F(r) = -k/r^3.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Central force motion can take place in three dimensions arbitrarily.
common_misconceptions.correct: Motion under a central force is strictly planar.
common_misconceptions.why: Conservation of angular momentum ensures that the position vector and velocity vector always lie in a fixed plane perpendicular to the constant angular momentum vector.

quick_revision: Central force magnitude depends only on distance r and points along the position vector.
Angular momentum L and areal velocity dA/dt are always conserved under central forces.
All central forces are conservative, allowing the definition of a potential energy function V(r).
Motion under central forces is always restricted to a single plane.
